explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, “…I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets…” (Exodus 34:1). Moses brings the chisel and the LORD brings the words. If it were up to me, those tablets would come back with a typo and a smudge.

Sealing isn't in the verse, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, chisels out the tablets, and the LORD says He will write on them. The words are the ones that were on the first tablets. Nobody mentions a stamp of approval, which is a relief, because my stamps used to come out blurry.

Polishing never comes up. The verse gives Moses, Israel's leader, the chiseling and gives the LORD the writing. Moses isn't buffing these tablets to a shine like a guy waxing his car on a Saturday. The LORD says He will write on them the words from the first tablets.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “No one may go up with you…” (Exodus 34:3). So Moses doesn't get a few helpers for the climb. It's just him, the tablets, and a mountain that doesn't care how tired he is.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “No one may go up with you; in fact, no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain…” (Exodus 34:3). Moses makes this climb alone. No buddy, no cheering section, and nobody to carry the second tablet.

explanations.answer: No flocks or herds may graze there
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, “…not even the flocks or herds may graze in front of the mountain” (Exodus 34:3). Not even the animals get to hang around. That's a clear mountain.
That's the opposite of what the LORD says. He says no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain (Exodus 34:3). So there's no camping up there. Whoever packed a tent can unpack it.

explanations.answer: A fence must go up there
explanations.explanation: A fence never comes up in these verses. The LORD simply says that no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain, and that not even the flocks or herds may graze in front of it (Exodus 34:3). The instruction is about who and what stays away. No lumber needed.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there…” (Exodus 34:5). He comes down and stands right there with Moses. Moses came up the mountain to be with Him, and now he is.

A pillar of fire is in the Bible, but it isn't the answer here. Back when Israel left Egypt, the LORD went before them by night in a pillar of fire (Exodus 13:21). Here on Sinai, the text says the LORD descended in a cloud (Exodus 34:5). Same LORD, different moment.
No whirlwind in this scene. The text says, “And the LORD descended in a cloud…” (Exodus 34:5). Then He stands with Moses. It's a calm picture, with no hat-flying weather.

Right on target. The LORD calls Himself “…compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Slow to anger, and overflowing with loving devotion. I take a lot longer than that to forgive somebody who touches my cookie dough.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD calls Himself “…compassionate and gracious, slow to anger…” (Exodus 34:6). He doesn't describe Himself as quick to anger. Compassion and grace come first in His own words.

explanations.answer: He is never angry at all
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not what He says. The LORD says He is “slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6). Slow isn't the same as never. In the very next verse He says He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished (Exodus 34:7).
That's right, baker. The LORD says He is “maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations” (Exodus 34:7). A thousand generations is a lot of family reunions. His love doesn't run out.
Not this time. The LORD says He is “maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations” (Exodus 34:7). So it's true, and it's a big number. That's love that keeps going and going.

Careful, friend, it's the opposite. The LORD says, “Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished…” (Exodus 34:7). He forgives, and He also won't leave the guilty unpunished. Both are in how He describes Himself.

Yes, that's right. The LORD says, “Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished…” (Exodus 34:7). So He does not say He will leave the guilty unpunished. It comes right after He describes Himself as forgiving.

explanations.answer: Go with us and forgive us
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says, “…please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin…” (Exodus 34:9). He asks for the LORD's company and for forgiveness. Moses doesn't ask for a bunch of extras.

explanations.answer: Send an angel ahead of us
explanations.explanation: There's no angel in his request. Moses says, “…please go with us” (Exodus 34:9). He asks for the LORD Himself to go along. He also asks for forgiveness in the same breath.

explanations.answer: Give us a king to lead us
explanations.explanation: A king never comes up here. Moses asks the Lord to go with them and to forgive their iniquity and sin (Exodus 34:9). Then he asks Him to take them as His inheritance. His request is about the LORD's company, not about adding a leader.

Not quite. The LORD says, “All the people among whom you live will see the LORD’s work…” (Exodus 34:10). So the people around Moses will notice, and it's not a quiet thing. He calls it “an awesome thing.”

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “All the people among whom you live will see the LORD’s work, for it is an awesome thing that I am doing with you” (Exodus 34:10). So they will notice. Nobody's going to miss it.

No, friend, the LORD says the opposite. He says, “Be careful not to make a treaty with the inhabitants of the land you are entering, lest they become a snare in your midst” (Exodus 34:12). So no treaties. This one is a firm no.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Be careful not to make a treaty with the inhabitants of the land you are entering…” (Exodus 34:12). He doesn't want Israel making treaties with them. He gives the reason in the same verse.
Yes, baker. The LORD says a treaty could make them “a snare in your midst” (Exodus 34:12). A snare is a trap. He's warning Israel before they walk into it.
Robbing isn't the worry here. The LORD says a treaty would let them become “a snare in your midst” (Exodus 34:12). A snare is a trap. It's not about stolen stuff.
Numbers aren't the issue in this verse. The LORD says a treaty could make them “a snare in your midst” (Exodus 34:12). A snare is a trap. His warning is about what the treaty could do.

That's right. The LORD says, “…you must tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, and chop down their Asherah poles” (Exodus 34:13). Tear down, smash, chop. That's three different verbs for one clear job.

The LORD says the opposite. He says, “…you must tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, and chop down their Asherah poles” (Exodus 34:13). Nothing is left standing in this list. It's tear down, smash and chop.

explanations.answer: Use them all for the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's not the plan in the verse. The LORD says to tear down the altars, smash the sacred stones and chop down the Asherah poles (Exodus 34:13). Nobody is told to reuse any of it. It all comes down.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…you must not worship any other god…” (Exodus 34:14). That's the reason for tearing everything down. He wants Israel's worship for Himself.
The word is god, not king. The LORD says, “…you must not worship any other god…” (Exodus 34:14). The command is about worship. It has nothing to do with a king.
Not nation, friend. The LORD says, “…you must not worship any other god…” (Exodus 34:14). The command is about worship, and it names other gods. That's why the altars and poles have to go.

Yes, baker. The LORD says that when those people “prostitute themselves to their gods and sacrifice to them, they will invite you, and you will eat their sacrifices” (Exodus 34:15). That's what a covenant with them could lead to. It starts as an invitation and ends up somewhere He warned about.

Actually, it's true. The LORD warns, “…they will invite you, and you will eat their sacrifices” (Exodus 34:15). That invitation is part of why He says not to make a covenant with them. It's a warning, and He gives it plainly.
That's right. The LORD says, “You shall make no molten gods for yourselves” (Exodus 34:17). It's one short sentence and it's clear. No molten gods, none.
That's not in the verse. The LORD says, “You shall make no molten gods for yourselves” (Exodus 34:17). The command is about making none in the first place. No melting plan is given.
No burying is mentioned. The LORD says, “You shall make no molten gods for yourselves” (Exodus 34:17). It's a short command, and it's about making none. No shovels needed.

That's right, baker. The text says, “So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights…” (Exodus 34:28). That's a long stay on one mountain. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant during that time.
Seven isn't it, friend. The text says, “So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights…” (Exodus 34:28). That's a lot longer than a week. Forty is the number.
Three days would be a short trip. The text says, “So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights…” (Exodus 34:28). Forty days, forty nights. That's a long time on one mountain.

Not this time, baker. The text says Moses was there “…without eating bread or drinking water” (Exodus 34:28). So no bread and no water for the whole forty days and forty nights. He was with the LORD that whole time.

That's right. The text says Moses was there with the LORD “forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water” (Exodus 34:28). So he ate no bread and drank no water. That's a long stretch.

Yes, baker. The text says, “…his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29). It was his face, not anything he was carrying or wearing. He came down from that mountain shining.
It wasn't the staff. The text says Moses's face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD (Exodus 34:29). Moses had two tablets in his hands. His face was what changed.
It wasn't his robe. The text says Moses's face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD (Exodus 34:29). So the glow is on his face. I'd have guessed a fancy outfit too.
Not quite, baker. The text says Moses “was unaware that his face had become radiant” (Exodus 34:29). He didn't know a thing about it. Everybody else could see it, and he couldn't.
Yes, baker. The text says Moses “was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29). He had no idea. The people who saw him knew before he did.

That's not what happened. Aaron, Moses' brother, and all the Israelites “were afraid to approach him” (Exodus 34:30). So they held back instead of rushing up. They saw the radiant face and kept their distance.
Yes, baker. Aaron, Moses' brother, and all the Israelites looked at Moses and “were afraid to approach him” (Exodus 34:30). So nobody rushed up. They stayed back.
That's right, baker. The text says, “But Moses called out to them…” (Exodus 34:31). He doesn't leave and he doesn't wait around. He calls them over, and they come.

explanations.answer: He hides in the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says Moses called out to the people, and Aaron and the leaders returned to him (Exodus 34:31). So he reaches out to them. He doesn't hide.

explanations.answer: He goes back up the mountain
explanations.explanation: He doesn't head back up. The text says, “But Moses called out to them; so Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him…” (Exodus 34:31). He calls them over, and they come. Then Moses speaks to them.
Yes, baker. The text says, “And after this all the Israelites came near…” (Exodus 34:32). First the leaders return, then everyone comes closer. The distance gets smaller.

Actually, it's true. The text says, “And after this all the Israelites came near…” (Exodus 34:32). After the leaders returned to Moses, everyone else did too. They had been keeping their distance, and now they don't.

explanations.answer: He passes on the LORD's commands
explanations.explanation: That's right. The text says, “…Moses commanded them to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai” (Exodus 34:32). He brings down what the LORD told him. All of it.

explanations.answer: He sends them back to their tents
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text. It says Moses “commanded them to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai” (Exodus 34:32). So he tells them what the LORD said. No one is sent away.

explanations.answer: He tells them to wait for Aaron
explanations.explanation: Waiting for Aaron isn't mentioned. Aaron, Moses' brother, is already there, since he returned with the leaders (Exodus 34:31). Moses commands them “to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai” (Exodus 34:32). That's the job.

Yes, baker. The text says, “…whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would remove the veil until he came out” (Exodus 34:34). So the veil comes off when he goes in. It stays off until he comes out.

It's the opposite. The text says that when Moses went in before the LORD, “he would remove the veil until he came out” (Exodus 34:34). So he takes it off, not leaves it on. He puts it back on afterward (Exodus 34:35).
No tightening in the text. It says Moses “would remove the veil until he came out” (Exodus 34:34). So the veil comes off while he's in there speaking with the LORD. Then it goes back on.
